hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to prominent horizontal or slightly diagonal linear structures, typically manifesting as distinct bars, ridges, edges, or strips that create a sharp visual boundary across the frame. These features—ranging from a monitor bezel, a dark tree branch, and metal pipes to a shoreline, door handle, or cabinet trim—are consistently dark-colored (typically black, dark brown, charcoal, or navy) or metallic, set against a generally lighter or lower-contrast background of white, beige, sky blue, or light grey. The activating element is characterized by its high aspect ratio and continuity, often separating distinct regions of the scene. The neuron remains invariant to the specific semantic identity of the object, surface texture, and lighting conditions, as long as the strong linear form and contrast are preserved. The linear feature typically extends across 50–100% of the image width and is positioned within the middle to upper 70% of the vertical frame.
